MISP contains a vulnerability in the cryptographic signature verification of protected events. When a MISP instance signs a protected event for synchronization, it strips all whitespace from the JSON body before computing the PGP signature (preg_replace("/\s+/", "", $data)). The receiving instance performs the same whitespace-stripping before verification. Because the signature covers only the whitespace-free representation, a network relay positioned between two MISP instances can insert whitespace characters into JSON object keys (effectively renaming fields) or into identifier values such as UUIDs, timestamps, and distribution fields without invalidating the signature. The receiving instance accepts the modified event as authentic.

The vulnerability affects the protected event synchronization path: event creation (EventsController::add), event editing (EventsController::edit), event viewing (EventsController::view1), and server-to-server pull synchronization (ServerSyncTool, Server model). An attacker with a network position to intercept and modify traffic between MISP instances can alter the semantic content of protected events while the PGP signature still validates, undermining the integrity guarantees that protected events are designed to provide.

The fix introduces two complementary mechanisms. First, a post-verification scan rejects any received body that contains whitespace in JSON keys (except under Galaxy cluster 'meta' keys) or in identifier-like values (uuid, id, timestamp, distribution, date). Second, a new exact-byte signature scheme (x-pgp-signature-v2) signs the body as transmitted, without whitespace normalization. MISP 3.0 and later peers exchange this exact-byte signature; older peers retain the legacy whitespace-stripped signature. A signature_version field is embedded in protected events so that a 3.0 receiver refuses a body carrying that marker if only the legacy signature is present. Both mechanisms together close the whitespace-injection vector while preserving backward compatibility with pre-3.0 instances.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, an unauthenticated user who can influence indexed event data could store attacker-controlled values in event fields. If another authenticated user who reviews the event selects the View Adaptive Response Invocations or View Adaptive Response Results workflow action from Event Actions, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the action. The unauthenticated user could then access or modify sensitive data and disrupt services available to the user who selects the action.
The vulnerability is possible because the affected Common Information Model workflow actions insert the orig_sid and orig_rid event-field values directly into searches without safely validating or quoting the values.
For more information see About workflow actions in Splunk Web (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/manage-knowledge-objects/knowledge-management-manual/10.2/workflow-actions/about-workflow-actions-in-splunk-web) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the ueba_finding_exclusion_edit capability could store attacker-controlled values in a User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) finding exclusion rule. With this access, the user could cause Splunk Enterprise Security to read stored credentials and modify lookups and knowledge objects.
The vulnerability is possible because the UEBA finding exclusion workflow does not escape user-controlled rule values before using them in generated SPL.
For more information see Create a finding exclusion rule using UEBA configuration page (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/administer/8.7/user-and-entity-behavior-analytics/finding-exclusions-in-splunk-enterprise-security/create-a-finding-exclusion-rule-using-ueba-configuration-page) and Users and roles for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/install/8.7/installation/users-and-roles-for-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the ueba_finding_exclusion_edit capability could create a finding exclusion rule that references an attacker-controlled lookup definition if the role also grants write access to globally shared lookup definitions, as the "ess_analyst" Splunk Enterprise Security role does. The User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) Content App could later include the lookup name in a search and run arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands with elevated permissions. With this access, the user who created the finding exclusion rule could expose stored credentials and other data outside the permissions assigned to the "ess_analyst" role.
The vulnerability is possible because UEBA finding exclusion processing does not safely quote lookup names before including them in SPL searches.
For more information see Finding exclusions in Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/administer/8.3/user-and-entity-behavior-analytics/finding-exclusions-in-splunk-enterprise-security) and Roles and knowledge objects in UEBA for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/administer/8.8/user-and-entity-behavior-analytics/ueba-content-app-for-on-premises/roles-and-knowledge-objects-in-ueba-for-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. In 3.10.3 and earlier, DependencyGraph._tree and triples recurse once per dependency edge without a depth bound, and get_cycle_path also lacks a visited-set termination guard. A deeply chained or cyclic attacker-controlled CoNLL or Malt-TAB dependency structure can raise RecursionError and abort a parse worker. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

MISP contains an authorization bypass in the correlations/eventCorrelations endpoint and the underlying correlation engines (Default and OnDemand). The CorrelationsController::eventCorrelations action did not verify that the requesting user was permitted to view the event specified by the event ID parameter. Any authenticated user could supply the ID of an event belonging to another organisation (distribution level 0, organisation-only) and receive its full correlation results, including attribute identifiers and values. Additionally, for events the user could partially view, the correlation engines filtered only the related (target) side of each correlation row and did not vet the queried event's own source attributes. As a result, correlations keyed by attributes hidden from the user (organisation-only attributes, attributes in sharing groups the user is not a member of, or attributes inside organisation-only objects) were returned with their IDs and values. The Default engine's related-event listing (used in events/view) also included events related solely through such hidden attributes. The vulnerability was reported by ENISA. Successful exploitation requires a valid authenticated session with any role and knowledge or enumeration of a target event ID. The security impact is disclosure of threat-intelligence attribute values (IP addresses, domain names, etc.) and attribute identifiers that the user is not authorised to see, as well as confirmation of the existence of otherwise invisible events.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: firewire: isight: bound the sample count to the packet payload

isight_packet() takes the frame count from the device iso packet and
checks it only against the device claimed iso length.

	count = be32_to_cpu(payload->sample_count);
	if (likely(count <= (length - 16) / 4))
		isight_samples(isight, payload->samples, count);

length is the iso header data_length. It can be up to 0xffff. So the
gate allows a count up to about 16379. isight_samples() then copies
count frames out of payload->samples into the PCM DMA buffer.

payload->samples holds only 2 * MAX_FRAMES_PER_PACKET values. The
device multiplexes two samples per frame. A count past
MAX_FRAMES_PER_PACKET reads past the payload. A count past the buffer
size writes past runtime->dma_area. The smallest PCM buffer is larger

keeps both the read and the write in range.

A malicious or faulty Apple iSight on the FireWire bus reaches this
during a normal capture.

Add the MAX_FRAMES_PER_PACKET bound to the gate.

An unauthenticated Remote Code Execution vulnerability was found in the survey passthrough routing and Data Import processing logic, in which a malicious user could potentially exploit it by manipulating HTTP requests to access an unintended controller route from a public survey context and by supplying a crafted file-path/stream parameter during import handling. If successfully exploited, this could allow the attacker to remotely execute arbitrary code on the REDCap server. The attacker does not have to be authenticated in order to exploit this, but exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash. This vulnerability exists in REDCap 13.3.0 and higher.

OwnPay is a self-hosted open-source payment gateway automation platform. In 0.2.0 and earlier, modules/gateways/alipay/AlipayGateway.php fails open when an Alipay callback lacks a signature or the merchant has no configured public key because verify(array $callbackData, array $credentials) falls back to an undefined mode credential that defaults to test mode, while verifyWebhook() returns true unconditionally. An unauthenticated request to POST /webhook/{gateway} can provide a pending order reference and matching amount, pass both verification gates without a valid payment signature, and cause the order and corresponding payment-received ledger entries to be marked completed. No fixed version is available as of this review.

X-Road is open-source data exchange layer software. Prior to 7.8.2 and 7.7.3, the Configuration Proxy uses attacker-controlled Content-location metadata from a validly signed federated global configuration part when constructing an output path without verifying that the resulting path remains inside the intended configuration output directory. A malicious or compromised federated ecosystem can provide an absolute path or directory traversal sequence during the normal refresh cycle, causing the Configuration Proxy to create a new file with attacker-controlled content under the permissions of the non-privileged xroad process. The vulnerability can poison downstream global configuration or create files in other writable locations, but it does not overwrite existing files. This issue is fixed in versions 7.8.2 and 7.7.3.

SharpIppNext is a .NET Standard library for building Internet Printing Protocol clients and servers. Prior to 4.1.0, server-side SharpIppNext implementations using SharpIppServer.ReceiveRequestAsync or SharpIppServer.ReceiveRawRequestAsync pass incoming data to IppProtocol.ReadIppRequestAsync in SharpIpp/Protocol/IppProtocol.cs, where ReadDocumentStream is enabled by default and the remaining document body is copied with CopyToAsync into a MemoryStream without a size limit. An unauthenticated remote client can send an arbitrarily large IPP document body, exhausting process memory and causing an out-of-memory failure or service termination. Client-only implementations using SharpIppClient are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.1.0.

MISP's EventDelegationsController delegateEvent method accepted a user-supplied sharing_group_id parameter without verifying that the requesting user was a member of the referenced sharing group. When a delegation request was submitted with distribution set to 4 (sharing-group distribution), the raw sharing_group_id value was stored directly into the EventDelegation record. The delegation view subsequently rendered the stored sharing group's name back to the requester. Because no authorization check was performed, any authenticated user with delegation permission could enumerate sharing group identifiers (by guessing sequential IDs or other values) and read the names of sharing groups to which their organisation did not belong, including hidden or restricted groups. Hidden, missing, and malformed identifiers were not distinguished in the response, but the successful case still leaked the group name. The vulnerability required an authenticated session with the perm_delegate capability and knowledge of a valid event ID to delegate. The security impact is limited to disclosure of sharing group names (a low-impact confidentiality breach) and does not grant access to the group's contents or modify any data.

MISP (Malware Information Sharing Platform) contains an authorization bypass in the SharingGroup model's captureSGExisting method. The authorization check used a logical AND condition that effectively exempted users with the sync permission (perm_sync) from the membership verification. Specifically, the original condition 'if (!checkIfAuthorised(...) && !perm_sync) return false' meant that any user holding the sync role would pass the check regardless of whether they were actually a member of the target sharing group.

A sync user who knows or can discover the UUID of a non-local sharing group could exploit this flaw through the /sharing_groups/add endpoint or by embedding a SharingGroup object in pushed sync data. The attacker could rewrite the sharing group record to add their own organisation as a member or insert an all_orgs server entry for their MISP instance, thereby gaining read access to all events contained in that group. This exposes threat intelligence data that was intended to be restricted to the group's legitimate members.

The vulnerability requires an authenticated account with the sync role and knowledge of a valid sharing group UUID. No user interaction is required. The impact is unauthorized disclosure of shared threat intelligence events and limited integrity modification of the sharing group record.

A vulnerability in the Object Linking and Embedding, 2nd Generation (OLE2) file parser for ClamAV could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to exceed the configured MaxScanTime and cause a DoS condition on an affected device.   This vulnerability is due to inefficiencies when parsing specifically formatted files with the OLE2 file parser. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by by sending a crafted Microsoft Compound File Binary (CFB) file to be scanned. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to effectively cause the ClamAV OLE2 parser to get into an infinite loop, resulting in a DoS condition on the affected software.

A vulnerability in the LZX data algorithm for Microsoft Compiled HTML Help (CHM) file scanning in ClamAV could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause a DoS condition on an affected device.
 This vulnerability is due to improper boundary checks when applying the LZX data algorithm to CHM files during the decoder stage, which may result in buffer overflow. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted CHM file for scanning. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the ClamAV scanning process to terminate, resulting in a DoS condition on the affected software.

A vulnerability in Object Linking and Embedding, 2nd Generation (OLE2) file parser for ClamAV could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause a DoS condition on an affected device.
 This vulnerability is due to logic error when parsing specifically formatted files with the OLE2 file parser. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by by sending a crafted Microsoft Compound File Binary (CFB) file to be scanned. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to allocate all available memory, causing the ClamAV scanning process to terminate, resulting in a DoS condition on the affected software.

A vulnerability in Microsoft Compiled HTML Help (CHM) file scanning of ClamAV could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause a DoS condition on an affected device.
 This vulnerability is due to a logic error when scanning the CHM file and following the internal file pointers. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted CHM file for scanning. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the ClamAV decode process to terminate due to an infinite loop, resulting in a DoS condition on the affected software.

OpenCTI is an open source platform for managing cyber threat intelligence knowledge and observables. Prior to 7.260706.0, the logsWorkerConfig GraphQL query is authorized with the broad CONNECTORAPI capability and returns Elasticsearch connection details including elasticsearch_username, elasticsearch_password, elasticsearch_api_key, the URL, index, proxy, and TLS-verification setting. A holder of any connector API bearer token can retrieve this credential material. If the returned credentials are valid and Elasticsearch is reachable, the caller can directly read, modify, or delete OpenCTI indices and audit history outside application-layer role, marking, organization, and audit controls, with the practical impact bounded by the credentials' privileges and network reachability. This issue is fixed in version 7.260706.0.

HtmlSanitizer is a .NET library for cleaning HTML fragments and documents from constructs that can lead to XSS attacks. One unauthenticated request can occupy a synchronous application worker for seconds, and concurrent requests can saturate all workers and sustain denial of service. This issue is fixed in versions 9.0.967 and 9.1.968-beta.

The FS Poster - WordPress Social media Auto Poster & Scheduler [Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Pinterest] plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to missing authorization to Unauthorized Social App Data Modification in all versions up to, and including, 8.0.1 This is due to missing authentication, nonce, and capability checks in the `standardFSApp()` function, which is registered on the `wp` action hook and executes on every frontend page load without any login or permission verification. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to insert arbitrary social network app records into the database, or overwrite the OAuth `client_id` and `client_secret` of existing social network connections, by supplying attacker-controlled values via the `fsp_app_redirect` and `app` GET parameters. An attacker can target a specific existing social app record for credential overwrite by supplying matching `social_network` and `slug` values, requiring no knowledge of internal record IDs, which disrupts scheduled social media posts and forces administrators to re-authenticate their connected accounts.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iio: adc: ad_sigma_delta: fix clear_pending_event for registerless devices

ad_sigma_delta_clear_pending_event() falls through to the status register
read path for devices with has_registers = false and no rdy_gpiod. For
such devices, ad_sd_read_reg() skips the address byte entirely and clocks
raw MISO bytes with no address phase — making it byte-for-byte identical
to reading conversion data. If a pending conversion result is present,
this partially consumes it and corrupts the data stream for the subsequent
ad_sd_read_reg() call in ad_sigma_delta_single_conversion().

Furthermore, with num_resetclks = 0 on these devices, data_read_len
evaluates to 0. If the clocked byte has bit 7 clear, pending_event is set
and the code attempts memset(data + 2, 0xff, 0 - 1), overflowing to
SIZE_MAX and corrupting the heap.

Fix by returning 0 immediately when neither rdy_gpiod nor has_registers
is set. This is safe for all current registerless devices: ad7191 and
ad7780 (with powerdown GPIO) are reset between conversions by CS
deassertion, so there is no stale result to drain; ad7780 (without
powerdown GPIO) and max11205 are continuously-converting and cycle ~DRDY
at the output data rate regardless of whether the previous result was
read, so the next falling edge fires naturally.

A future registerless device that holds ~DRDY asserted until data is read
would be broken by this early return and would require either
num_resetclks set or a rdy-gpio.

The same heap corruption is reachable on any device with rdy_gpiod set
but num_resetclks = 0: if the GPIO indicates a pending event, the drain
path executes memset(data + 2, 0xff, 0 - 1) regardless of has_registers.
Add an explicit data_read_len == 0 guard after the pending event check;
the stale result is then consumed by the first ad_sd_read_reg() call in
ad_sigma_delta_single_conversion().

Fumasoft Fumeng Cloud contains a SQL injection vulnerability in the AjaxMethod.ashx endpoint that allows unauthenticated remote attackers to inject arbitrary SQL through the Name parameter of the getEmpByname action without any authentication. Attackers can exploit UNION-based SQL injection techniques against the Microsoft SQL Server backend to extract, disclose, and modify database contents, with potential for further compromise of the underlying server. Exploitation evidence was first observed by the Shadowserver Foundation on 2023-10-18.

DBLTek GoIP devices (models GoIP 1, 4, 8, 16, and 32) contain an undocumented vendor backdoor in the Telnet administrative interface that allows remote authentication as an undocumented user via a proprietary challenge–response scheme which is fundamentally flawed. Because the challenge response can be computed from the challenge itself, a remote attacker can authenticate without knowledge of a secret and obtain a root shell on the device. This can lead to persistent remote code execution, full device compromise, and arbitrary control of the device and any managed services. The firmware used within these devices was updated in December 2016 to make this vulnerability more complex to exploit. However, it is unknown if DBLTek has taken steps to fully mitigate.

Seeyon A6 collaborative office automation platform contains an unauthenticated SQL injection vulnerability in the attach_ids parameter of the file attachment download endpoint that allows remote attackers to extract arbitrary database contents without prior authentication. Attackers can inject UNION-based SQL statements through the attach_ids request parameter in downloadAtt.jsp to retrieve sensitive information including credentials and system configuration data. Exploitation evidence was first observed by the Shadowserver Foundation on 2023-10-17.

ZPanel includes a helper binary named zsudo, intended to allow restricted privilege escalation for administrative tasks. However, when misconfigured in /etc/sudoers, zsudo can be invoked by low-privileged users to execute arbitrary commands as root. This flaw enables local attackers with shell access to escalate privileges by writing a payload to a writable directory and executing it via zsudo. The vulnerability is particularly impactful in post-exploitation scenarios following web server compromise, where the attacker inherits access to zsudo.

FreeFloat FTP Server contains multiple critical design flaws that allow unauthenticated remote attackers to upload arbitrary files to sensitive system directories. The server accepts empty credentials, defaults user access to the root of the C:\ drive, and imposes no restrictions on file type or destination path. These conditions enable attackers to upload executable payloads and .mof files to locations such as system32 and wbem\mof, where Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) automatically processes and executes them. This results in remote code execution with SYSTEM-level privileges, without requiring user interaction.

Amlib’s NetOpacs webquery.dll contains a stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability triggered by improper handling of HTTP GET parameters. Specifically, the application fails to enforce bounds on input supplied to the app parameter, allowing excessive data to overwrite memory structures including the Structured Exception Handler (SEH). Additionally, malformed parameter names followed by an equals sign may result in unintended control flow behavior. This vulnerability is exposed through IIS and affects legacy Windows deployments

Issue summary: A QUIC server that rejects a stream opened by the peer may
retain that stream's state for the lifetime of the connection if the peer
resets the stream before the rejection is signalled, even though the peer's
stream credit is returned.

Impact summary: A remote client that completes a QUIC handshake can repeatedly
open and reset streams, causing server memory to grow without bound until the
process runs out of memory and every connection on it is lost. This is a
Denial of Service.

CWE: CWE-401: Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime

Description: QUIC servers track each stream the peer opens. When the incoming
stream policy rejects a stream, OpenSSL schedules a STOP_SENDING frame, marks
the stream deleted and returns the peer's stream credit. A deleted stream is
collected only once its receive part is fully drained, which for a rejected
stream means the STOP_SENDING has been acknowledged. If the peer sends
RESET_STREAM first, the reset cancels the pending STOP_SENDING, so it is never
sent or acknowledged and the stream is never collected.

The default configuration reaches this path. Once a connection has a default
stream, meaning the application has read from or written to the connection as
the tutorial server does, the effective incoming stream policy rejects streams
the application does not accept. Applications that set the REJECT policy
explicitly are affected too.

Each retained stream costs about 300 bytes, and the peer's stream credit
window paces how quickly they accumulate. A client that keeps the connection
open and keeps opening and resetting streams grows server memory without
bound. The severity is Low because growth is slow, needs a long-lived
connection, and causes no memory corruption or disclosure.

FIPS impact: no
The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

OpenCTI is an open source platform for managing cyber threat intelligence knowledge and observables. Prior to 7.260722.0, the GraphQL endpoint accepts query operations over HTTP GET because CSRF prevention is disabled (csrfPrevention: false), placing the complete GraphQL query and its arguments in the request URL. Server and reverse-proxy logs, browser history, and shared caches can retain sensitive filters, marking-restricted identifiers, and investigation search arguments, allowing a person with access to those records to recover legitimate users' query contents. GraphQL mutations are not accepted over GET, and the issue does not permit code execution. This issue is fixed in version 7.260722.0.

N-able N-central before 2026.4.1 HF3 checks only a view permission for ServerII2 operations that write device execution configuration. An authenticated user with view-only access to a device can set configuration that the Windows agent on that device acts on.

OpenCTI is an open source platform for managing cyber threat intelligence knowledge and observables. Prior to 7.260624.0, an Organization Administrator with VIRTUAL_ORGANIZATION_ADMIN and KNOWLEDGE_KNUPDATE can use organizationFieldPatch to replace the administered organization's grantable_groups without a SETTINGS_SETACCESSES authorization check. The administrator can add the built-in Administrators group to that grant scope and then bypass the grantable_groups guard added by the incomplete CVE-2026-44730 remediation to add their own account to Administrators. Membership grants the BYPASS capability after session cache refresh, escalating the tenant-scoped account to global administrator with access across organizations, users, settings, markings, connectors, and ingestion. This issue is fixed in version 7.260624.0.

NVIDIA Model Optimizer for Linux and Windows contains a vulnerability where an attacker could cause a deserialization of untrusted data. A successful exploit of this vulnerability might lead to code execution, data tampering, denial of service, and information disclosure.

OpenCTI is an open source platform for managing cyber threat intelligence knowledge and observables. Prior to 7.260701.0, the caseIncidentAdd, caseRfiAdd, and caseRftAdd GraphQL mutations require only authentication and do not require a capability check. An authenticated user with reader-level permissions can therefore create incident, request-for-information, and request-for-takedown case objects regardless of the user's assigned role, causing unauthorized changes to platform data. This issue is fixed in version 7.260701.0.

OpenCTI is an open source platform for managing cyber threat intelligence knowledge and observables. Prior to 7.260715.0, a ProfileQuery response can expose the user's TOTP MFA secret after activation. A person who can access the profile response can recover the secret, enroll a duplicate authenticator, and generate valid one-time codes, undermining the account's second-factor protection. This issue is fixed in version 7.260715.0.

OpenCTI is an open source platform for managing cyber threat intelligence knowledge and observables. Prior to 7.260513.0, Draft Workspace identifiers are accepted without verifying that the authenticated user can access the referenced draft. Any authenticated user can enumerate draftWorkspaces, use a disclosed DRAFT_ID with draftWorkspaceEntities to read unpublished reports, descriptions, observables, and other staged intelligence, or place the identifier in the opencti-draft-id header and run mutations that inject entities and relationships into another user's private workspace. The flaw permits cross-user disclosure and tampering but does not cause a denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 7.260513.0.

Directus is a real-time API and App dashboard for managing SQL database content. Prior to 12.3.1, Directus allows an authenticated non-admin with update permission on directus_shares to modify user_created, role, item, and collection on an existing owned share because authorization checks the pre-update row and does not revalidate the merged row. The update path does not force user_created to the acting user or rerun share access checks when item or collection changes. Setting user_created and role to administrator identifiers causes guest share authentication to derive administrator accountability from both fields, exposing data reachable from the shared item beyond the owner and share role permissions. The issue requires update permission on directus_shares, an item the account can share, and knowledge of administrator user and role identifiers, and it does not issue an administrator token or provide write or availability impact. This issue is fixed in version 12.3.1.

SeaweedFS before 4.42 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability in the VolumeServer.FetchAndWriteNeedle gRPC method that allows unauthenticated attackers to bypass the incomplete CVE-2026-73080 fix. Attackers can supply crafted replicas[].url entries or an azure_endpoint to make the volume server send requests with controlled tokens and bodies to internal services and metadata addresses.

Zohocorp ManageEngine DDI Central versions below 6301 is affected by an authorization bypass and PowerShell command injection vulnerability that allowed authenticated non-administrative users to target unauthorized Windows DHCP subnets and potentially execute arbitrary commands on managed Windows DHCP servers through crafted DNS suffix values.

Zohocorp ManageEngine DDI Central versions below 6301 is affected by an authorization bypass vulnerability that allowed authenticated non-administrative users to modify Windows DHCP filter-list configurations across unauthorized clusters.

Zohocorp ManageEngine DDI Central versions below 6301 is affected by an authentication bypass vulnerability in Windows DNS and DHCP agent synchronization APIs, allowing unauthenticated user to impersonate onboarded Windows servers and perform unauthorized DNS and DHCP modifications.
Zohocorp ManageEngine DDI Central versions below 6301 is affected by a PowerShell injection vulnerability due to insufficient validation of user-supplied TXT record values in Windows DNS operations.

Docker Sandboxes reuses existing state and configuration directories without verifying their ownership. If sbx or sandboxd is run as root with HOME or, on Linux, XDG_STATE_HOME pointing to an attacker-controlled location, a local unprivileged user can substitute control-plane sockets and configuration trusted by the root process, potentially executing commands as root. Exploitation requires a privileged invocation with an attacker-influenced environment. The issue affects Linux and macOS and is fixed in version 0.53.0.

Improper verification of the source of a communication channel vulnerability in Opera Neon on macOS and Windows allows a malicious browser extension to take control of the browser by sending commands through MCP Hub to the built-in Browser Operator extension. This issue affects Opera Neon MCP Hub extension: 0.0.1.

Next.js is a React framework for building full-stack web applications. From 15.0.0 until 15.5.29 and 16.4.5, Next.js applications that use NextResponse to set cookies on Edge runtime routes expose the internal x-middleware-set-cookie header in the public response. This affects App Router route handlers and Pages Router Edge API routes. The header duplicates each cookie value and its attributes, so JavaScript already running on the same origin can read values that the Set-Cookie header marks HttpOnly, including sensitive session tokens set on an affected response. This issue is fixed in versions 16.4.5 and 15.5.29.

In Progress® Telerik® UI for ASP.NET Core versions `2015.1.318` through `2026.3.1015`, the server-side FilterParser processes nested expressions in untrusted filter parameters through recursive parsing without a recursion-depth limit, while FilterLexer does not enforce an input-length limit. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this if the application exposes an endpoint using DataSourceRequest model binding that is reachable without authentication. Deeply nested filters can trigger parsing errors during model binding or cause `StackOverflowException`. This issue is fixed in version `2026.4.1111`.

In Progress® Telerik® UI for ASP.NET MVC versions `2012.2.710` through `2026.3.1015`, server-side filter processing does not properly validate descriptor types, null values, or stack state in FilterNodeVisitor and does not catch FilterParserException within the affected assembly. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this if the application exposes an endpoint reachable without authentication that accepts crafted filter parameters. Affected requests can trigger uncaught cast, null-reference, or empty-stack exceptions and return HTTP 500. The report does not demonstrate worker-process termination or disruption of unrelated requests. The issue is fixed in version `2026.4.1111`.

Cudy TR3000 before 2.5.42 contains a command injection vulnerability that allows authenticated administrators to execute commands as root by injecting newlines into the IPsec keyexchange field of the vpn.set_conf RPC method. Attackers can append a second leftupdown directive to ipsec.conf, which StrongSwan's updown plugin runs as root when an attacker-controlled peer establishes the CHILD_SA.

Flowise through 3.1.4 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that allows authenticated attackers with chatflows or agentflows create/update permissions to bypass the Custom Function sandbox's SSRF protection by requiring a module subpath inside an allowlisted package, such as axios/dist/node/axios.cjs or node-fetch/lib/index.js, which evades the vm2 mock table and returns an unwrapped HTTP client that skips the checkDenyList validation. Attackers can issue arbitrary GET and POST requests with attacker-controlled bodies via POST /api/v1/node-custom-function to reach loopback and internal-network addresses or the cloud metadata endpoint, enabling network mapping, credential disclosure, and state changes on internal services.

Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 through 6.3.7, with a MySQL or MariaDB database, TlsMode=verify-full and no TlsCaFile, does not verify the database server's certificate's issuer or name when the connection is one that MariaDB Connector/C treats as local - Server= set to 127.0.0.1, ::1 or localhost (on Linux a Unix socket), to . on Windows (a named pipe), or to a comma-separated list of servers that holds such an element - which allows a local attacker who can stand in for the database server, for example by listening on its port while it is stopped or restarting, to receive the database sign-in, the password included, and to read and modify the traffic between hMailServer and its database. hMailServer applied verify-full by turning the client's certificate verification on without a CA file, but MariaDB Connector/C 3.4.1 and later, on a connection they treat as local and with no CA file, accept any certificate within its validity period that is self-signed or sent with its own root, for any name (Connector/C 3.4.2 to 3.4.10 also one whose issuer they cannot find), so the client accepted the certificate an impostor made, asked no proof of the password and allowed a switch to an authentication method that sends the password unhashed, while hmailserver --check-database said the certificate had been checked against the system's trust store and the application log that it had been checked. The Windows builds bundle Connector/C 3.4.9 (6.3.4 to 6.3.6) and 3.4.11 (6.3.7); on Linux the distribution's client is used, and Connector/C 3.3 and 3.4.0 and Oracle's MySQL client are not affected. The configuration is not the default: TlsMode defaults to prefer, which checks no certificate.

Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.25 through 6.3.7 on Windows, with a PostgreSQL database, the connection's sslmode require, verify-ca or verify-full, and a root certificate file named by PostgreSQLSslRootCert (from 6.2.25) or, with TlsMode=verify-full and neither PostgreSQL key set, by TlsCaFile (from 6.3.4), hands the file's name to libpq as bytes in the system's ANSI code page (up to 6.3.5 as Latin-1 bytes, which on code page 1252 are the code page's own for U+00A0 to U+00FF), and libpq looks for the file by those bytes and then hands the same bytes to OpenSSL, whose file opening on Windows reads a name as UTF-8 first and opens the file at that reading when one is there. When every byte of the name outside ASCII also reads as UTF-8 - for example U+00C3 U+00A9, the bytes C3 A9 on code page 1252, which are U+00E9 in UTF-8 - the database server's certificate was checked against the file at that other name whenever one was there, which allows a local attacker who can create that file but cannot change the configured one, as any user can by default beside a file an administrator keeps under ProgramData, or beside a folder directly under the system drive's root whose permissions the administrator restricted, and who can intercept the connection to the database server or stand in for it, to have hMailServer trust a certificate authority of the attacker's own and read and modify the traffic between hMailServer and its database, the database password included; the file alone, holding no authority that issued the database server's certificate, stops hMailServer from connecting to its database. The same applies in 6.3.4 through 6.3.7 to TlsCaFile when an Oracle MySQL client library has been put in place of the bundled MariaDB Connector/C, since that client opens the file through OpenSSL in the same way; the bundled MariaDB Connector/C opens the file in the code page and is not affected, and neither are the Linux builds. The configuration is not the default: by default no root certificate file is named.

Vvveb through 1.0.8.6 contains an SQL injection vulnerability because the @KEYS(:each) macro emits PHP array keys as backtick-quoted INSERT column names without escaping, and several procedures in admin/sql/mysqli/product.sql and admin_auth_token.sql omit the @FILTER guard. Authenticated back-office users able to save products can submit product_<feature> POST array keys containing backticks to redirect bound values into unexposed columns or break SQL statements.

The TouchOffice API `clerkList` endpoint appears to return sensitive clerk authentication data, including clerk PINs and iButton serial numbers. If the endpoint is accessible to callers who do not require access to these values, the API exposes reusable authentication material beyond the minimum information necessary for clerk-list functionality.

Pyrus Sync for Windows contains a local privilege escalation vulnerability caused by missing authorization controls in its PyrusSyncService Windows service, which allow an attacker with unprivileged access to create files using the ISyncService contract.

OpenAM before 16.1.4 fails to enforce PKCE in the OAuth 2.0 device authorization flow, never validating the code verifier when device codes are exchanged for tokens. Attackers who obtain an approved device code from client logs or shared device storage can redeem it for access and ID tokens to impersonate the user.

Unverified ownership in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.7 allows a local authenticated user to run code as the mail server's service account or as an administrator when setup installs into, or upgrades, a program folder that accounts other than the administrators could write before, such as one made beforehand at the root of a drive. 6.3.7 fixed CVE-2026-107571 by giving the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel permissions that only administrators may change, but setup refused nothing that was already in them, or in the folders that hold the event script, the add-ons and the database scripts: a program, a library, a script or a settings file that another account owns, or whose own permissions let another account change it, is kept with that owner and those permissions, which the hardening of the folders does not take away. Setup then runs programs from Bin with the administrator's elevated rights, and the service, which runs as LocalSystem or as its virtual account, runs them and the event script, so that a library such an account placed in Bin is loaded in place of the system's; the account can still change the file after the installation. The default installation under Program Files is not affected.

Inefficient algorithmic complexity in the JSON reader of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.6 and 6.3.7 allows a remote attacker to hold the server's mail delivery threads or its REST API's worker threads, making mail delivery, the REST API and the webmail unavailable. 6.3.6 fixed CVE-2026-107574, in which reading a JSON object searched the member names already read for each new name, by keeping the names in a hash set; the set uses the standard library's hash, which takes no secret, so member names chosen to fall in one bucket of it still cost time growing with the square of their number. Against the released reader, one such object of 16 MB took about 5 seconds to read in the Linux build, and one of under 6 MB about 23 seconds in the Windows build, where objects of the same sizes with other names took under a tenth of a second. A remote unauthenticated attacker reaches the reader by mailing such an object as a TLS-RPT report, up to 16 MB once decompressed, to a hosted domain's report mailbox, where an administrator has set one; it is read on a mail delivery thread (ten by default), and those threads deliver all mail, local and outbound, so a stream of such reports stops all delivery for as long as it continues. It is also reached without an account through the reply to a password-protected message, with the message's link alone, where the REST API is on (it is off by default) and a public base URL for such links is set; and by any account through the webmail's routes granted 16 MB, and by an application's API key through the send API. Each such request holds one of the REST API's four worker threads, in the process that also serves SMTP, IMAP and POP3.

Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.3.7 on Windows hands OpenSSL the names of its own TLS files - the listeners' certificates, chains, private keys and Diffie-Hellman parameters, a port's client-certificate CA file (from 6.2.19), the object store's CA file (from 6.3.4) and the ACME client's keys and certificates - as Latin-1 bytes, which on code page 1252 are the code page's own for U+00A0 to U+00FF, and OpenSSL's file opening on Windows reads a name as UTF-8 first and opens the file at that reading when it is there, or creates it there when its folder is. When every byte of a configured name outside ASCII also reads as UTF-8 - for example U+00C3 U+00A9, the bytes C3 A9, which are U+00E9 in UTF-8 - the server used the file at that other name whenever one was there, which allows a local attacker who can create that file or its folder but cannot change the configured one, as any user can by default beside a file an administrator keeps under ProgramData, to have a port that logs on by client certificate (from 6.2.25) accept certificates from a certificate authority of the attacker's own and so sign in over the network as any mailbox without its password; to have the server trust such an authority for its object store and, intercepting that connection, read and modify the messages it stores; to receive the private keys the ACME client writes, the key of a certificate issued for the server's names among them; or to keep TLS ports from starting. The configuration is not the default: by default these files have names in ASCII, client certificates are off on every port, and the object store and ACME are off. The Linux builds are not affected.

Misinterpretation of SQL statement text in the database layer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.3.7 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to have a failed database write reported to the server as successful. The layer answers a failed statement as a success when it finds the marker [IGNORE-ERRORS], which is meant only for the server's own schema statements (its upgrade scripts and the database log's tables), and statements carry values from outside - an envelope address, the user name of a failed logon, a message's headers - in their text on MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL, and in the batches of the database log on every engine. Up to 6.2.18 the marker was honoured anywhere in a statement, a value included, on MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL. From 6.2.19 it was honoured only inside a comment, but the layer read a backslash inside a string literal as an escape, which SQL Server, SQL Server Compact and PostgreSQL with standard_conforming_strings on (its default) do not, so that on those engines a value holding a backslash could make the layer take part of the statement's literals for statement text and find the marker there: on PostgreSQL from 6.3.3 for every statement carrying an outside value that holds a backslash, with no setting changed for a message delivered into a local mailbox (through an internationalised (SMTPUTF8) envelope sender) and for the IP range an auto-ban writes (named after the user name of the failed logon), and on SQL Server and SQL Server Compact for the database log, when the server logs to the database (logging is off, and the log device is files, by default). A statement run outside a transaction that then failed - a constraint, a deadlock, a lock or statement timeout, a full disk, and up to 6.2.18 a lost connection - was answered as a success, and its caller went on as if the row had been written: a message delivered into a local mailbox could be counted as delivered with no row to show it and no failure notice to its sender, and a message accepted with 250 could be left with no queue row and never delivered (up to 6.2.18, and on PostgreSQL from 6.3.3 when every recipient's address carries the marker too, which needs an address that takes any local part); an auto-ban whose IP range was not written could be logged and counted as applied, with no error reported, while the address stayed unbanned; and message metadata (written only when message indexing is on), entries of the database log and rows of features an administrator turns on could be lost without an error. On MySQL/MariaDB up to 6.2.18 the caller was handed whatever identifier the client library still held for the connection - 0, or that of an insert its last successful statement made, in whatever table - under which a queued message's recipients were then written, so that another message still in the queue could be delivered to them as well. This flaw gives a value no way to change what a statement does, and no privilege is gained.

The auto-ban of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.3.7 can be kept from banning an address after repeated failed logons, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker who can connect from two or more addresses to go on guessing account passwords - over SMTP AUTH, IMAP and POP3, and over ManageSieve, CalDAV/CardDAV and the REST API where those are turned on (off by default) - without being banned. When the failed logons counted from one address reach MaxInvalidLogonAttempts (3 by default), the server clears that address's count, saves an IP range that refuses the address for AutoBanMinutes (60 by default) and drops the connection. The range is named "Auto-ban: " followed by the user name of the logon that reached the limit, and no two ranges may have the same name. The server chooses the name by checking candidates as written - the name, then the name with a number, a random suffix or a GUID added - and only then cuts it to the 100 characters the database column holds, so that with a user name of 90 characters or more every candidate is the same once cut. While one range named after such a user name stands, every later ban named after a user name with the same first 90 characters therefore fails at the database: no range is saved, the address is not refused, and, its count having already been cleared, it is given the next full set of attempts. A user name of 78 to 89 characters makes later bans fail in the same way: from the second, the third or the twelfth on, depending on its length and the database, or, from 78 to 85 characters, by chance. An attacker who has once had an address banned under such a name can in this way keep guessing passwords from any other address, ending each set of attempts with a logon under a name of that kind; each failed save is reported in the server's error log (as the database error HM5032, and from 6.2.19 also as HM6099). On SQL Server a user name holding characters outside the database's code page has the same effect at any length, because the check compared names in that code page; that save is refused by the server's own check of the name, with no database error, and is reported only from 6.2.19 (HM6099). A user name holding a NUL character, which the web services listener's HTTP Basic sign-in (off by default) carries from 6.3.3 and, on the Linux builds, IMAP LOGIN, offered as installed, from 6.3.0, makes bans fail at any length: on MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL the statements that check the name and save the range end at the character, so that every ban named after such a name fails, from the first and from a single address, and, its count having already been cleared, the address is given the next full set of attempts; on SQL Server and SQL Server Compact the name is bound only as far as the character, so that while one range under the part before it stands, every later ban named after such a name fails. On SQL Server, and on MySQL and MariaDB for an account whose local part has nine characters or more, a guess at the account can itself carry a name of that kind, since those databases find an account under its address followed by spaces (and SQL Server also under one holding characters its comparison ignores), so that not even a MaxInvalidLogonAttempts of 1, which bans each failed logon under the name it gave, avoids it there.

SQL injection in the database layer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.2.18, when the server uses MySQL/MariaDB or PostgreSQL, allows a remote attacker to alter SQL statements the server runs. On those two engines parameters are not bound: SQLStatement::GenerateFromCommand wrote each value into the statement's text as a quoted literal with a separate string replacement over the whole text per parameter, so a value holding the name of a parameter substituted after it had that name replaced, inside the value, by the later value with its own quotes, which ended the literal early and placed the later value in the statement as SQL. The row the server writes for each recipient of a queued message carries the recipient's address twice, so in the default configuration an authenticated user who may send mail reaches it by sending to an address of their choosing. A remote unauthenticated sender reaches the same statement through a message the server sends to the envelope sender, such as a delivery failure notice or an automatic reply, and, when greylisting or message indexing is enabled (both are off by default), through the greylisting record's envelope addresses or through the message metadata the server stores for IMAP SORT, which carries four header fields of a received message. An altered statement runs with the privileges of the server's database account; on PostgreSQL, whose client call runs every statement in the text it is given, further statements can follow it, while on MySQL/MariaDB, where one statement is run per call, the change is confined to the statement it is in. SQL Server and SQL Server Compact, where parameters are bound, are not affected.

The auto-ban of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.0 through 6.3.3, with a MySQL or MariaDB database, can be kept from banning an address after repeated failed logons, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to go on guessing account passwords from a single address without being banned. The server makes its MySQL tables in MySQL's utf8 character set, which holds no character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, sends its statements as UTF-8 over a utf8mb4 connection and leaves the database's default strict mode in place. From 6.2.0 it decodes the user name of a SASL PLAIN logon as UTF-8, so the name can hold such a character. When the failed logons counted from one address reach MaxInvalidLogonAttempts (3 by default), the server clears that address's count, saves an IP range named "Auto-ban: " followed by the user name of the logon that reached the limit, and drops the connection. If such a character is in the part of the user name that the range's name keeps (the name is cut to 100 characters), the database refuses the range: no range is saved, the address is not refused, and, its count having already been cleared, it is given the next full set of attempts. An attacker can in this way spend all but the last attempt of each set on password guesses, and make the last under such a name. On Windows, POP3 AUTH PLAIN reaches it on a server as installed, and IMAP AUTHENTICATE PLAIN where IMAP SASL authentication is turned on (off by default); on Windows and on Linux (from 6.3.0), SMTP AUTH PLAIN reaches it where plain-text authentication is allowed (off by default), and ManageSieve and CardDAV where they are turned on (off by default). Each failed save is reported in the server's error log. A database whose strict mode has been turned off stores the character as a question mark and makes the first such ban, but refuses every later ban named after the same user name, or after one holding other such characters in their place, as a duplicate while the first stands, since the server cannot look up a name holding such a character there.

The sign-in of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.22-pre2 through 6.3.7 takes for an account names that are not its address but under which the database's own comparison finds it, while the per-name lockout and the compromised-account hold are kept by the name as the client gave it. This allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to go on guessing an account's password beyond the lockout's threshold, and anyone who has the password of an account held for review to sign in to it. The per-name lockout (from 6.2.22-pre2; AccountLockoutThreshold in hMailServer.ini, 0, off, by default) locks a name after repeated failed sign-ins. The hold (from 6.3.4, where the compromised-account detection is set to enforce, which is not the default) refuses an account judged to have been taken over. Both are asked, before the password, of the name the client gave: trimmed, in lower case and with a domain alias or the default domain applied. The account whose password the sign-in then checks is whichever one the database finds under that name. The databases find an account under spellings that this key counts apart. MySQL and MariaDB find it under one with accented letters in place of plain ones, and MariaDB 11.8, in a database made before 6.3.4, also under one with full-width letters, with a single letter in place of a pair of plain ones, or with characters its comparison ignores in any number. SQL Server and SQL Server Compact find it under one with full-width letters or with characters their comparison ignores in any number, and SQL Server also under one with a single letter in place of a pair of plain ones, with a character of Latin-1 in place of a digit and, for an address holding letters of Latin-1 outside ASCII, under those letters in the other case, and, under an accent-insensitive collation, with accented letters. PostgreSQL finds it under one holding a letter whose lower case under the database's locale is a plain letter, and, for an address holding letters outside ASCII, under those letters in the other case; on the build for musl (from 6.3.6) the server's own lower case folds nearly all of these too. On every database, a domain alias saved with white space at the end of its name gives such a spelling too, and on every database but PostgreSQL so does an account's bare local part where the default domain was saved with spaces at its end and no other white space (neither is the default). Each such spelling has a lockout threshold of its own, so the lockout limits the guesses at an account only to its threshold times the number of the account's spellings. That is far beyond any threshold for most addresses on MySQL and MariaDB, and without limit on SQL Server, on SQL Server Compact, the database the Windows installer uses by default, and before 6.3.4 on MariaDB 11.8. A locked name is got round under another spelling. A held account is signed in to under another spelling with its password over IMAP, POP3 and SMTP AUTH, and, where they are turned on (off by default), over ManageSieve, the REST API and the webmail. IMAP LOGIN, offered as installed, carries such spellings on MySQL, MariaDB and SQL Server Compact, and, on SQL Server and PostgreSQL, for some addresses; the sign-ins that carry a name as UTF-8 carry them for the others on SQL Server, and on PostgreSQL for those holding one of the plain letters another letter lowers to or a letter outside ASCII with another case. The same lookup mapped to accounts the names given by an OAuth 2.0 token, a client certificate, a Kerberos ticket and an OpenID Connect or SAML identity provider, where those are set up (none is by default), so that a name an issuer gave to one party could sign in to another's account; OAuth 2.0 tokens were mapped so from 6.2.0, before the per-name lockout existed. A name holding a NUL character, carried from 6.3.0 on Linux and 6.3.3 on Windows, failed the statement on MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL.

Improper link resolution in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.7 allows a local authenticated user to run code as the mail server's service account or as an administrator when the path to the program folder passes through a junction, a symbolic link or a mount point that the user controls or that every user may change, such as a junction made at the root of a drive, which takes the root's permissions, or through a folder that every user may rename. Setup installed the programs through any such link without first checking who controls it, or whether a folder above the program folder may be renamed, and the service is registered to run the programs by that path, so the programs are installed where a link another account controls leads, or that account can later make the path lead to a folder it controls; the service, which runs as LocalSystem or as its virtual account, and the programs administrators run from Bin are then started from there. 6.3.7's fix for CVE-2026-107571 does not cover this: its hardening of the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel does not change a folder reached through a link that the administrators do not alone control, and setup does not refuse such a path: it installs through the link and at most reports afterwards that the folders could not be hardened. The default installation under Program Files is not affected.

Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 through 6.3.7, with a MySQL or MariaDB database and TlsMode=verify-full, does not hand the database client the CA file that TlsCaFile names when the file's name contains a character outside ASCII on Linux, or above U+00FF on Windows, which allows an attacker who can intercept the connection to the database server to read and modify the traffic between hMailServer and its database, by presenting, with MariaDB Connector/C 3.4.2 to 3.4.10 as the client, a certificate from any authority, its own included, for any name, and otherwise a certificate for the database server's name issued by any certificate authority in the system's trust store. The server converted the name for the client with the C runtime's conversion in the C locale, which gives an empty string for such a name, and then set no CA file at all, without an error, while certificate verification stayed on, so the client - MariaDB Connector/C, bundled on Windows and the distribution's on Linux - verified the certificate of a database server over the network against the system's trust store instead of the configured CA; Connector/C 3.4.2 to 3.4.10 (bundled on Windows in 6.3.4 to 6.3.6) went further and, with no CA file, took a certificate within its dates whose issuer it could not find, for any name, with neither its chain nor its name checked and no password proof, when the server offered first a sign-in method that hashes the password, which an attacker in the middle chooses (MariaDB's CONC-853, fixed in Connector/C 3.4.11), and Connector/C 3.4 accepted from a MariaDB 11.4 or later server a certificate the store did not vouch for when that server proved it held the account's password; on a connection it treats as local (127.0.0.1, ::1, a Unix socket, a named pipe, and localhost on Windows), Connector/C 3.4.1 and later checked neither the certificate's issuer nor its name, so that a local attacker able to stand in for the database server could present any certificate within its dates of its own making. The settings line of hmailserver --check-database still named the configured file, and the application log said the certificate had been checked. With MariaDB Connector/C 3.4.1 to 3.4.9 as the client - bundled on Windows in 6.3.4 to 6.3.6, and the client of Linux distributions that have not patched it - the missing CA file also met the precondition of CVE-2026-107819, so that a certificate issued for any other name by a trusted authority was enough to obtain the database password. On Linux the file was found only when the server ran on glibc under a locale whose character set holds the name's characters (a UTF-8 locale, or a legacy 8-bit one the system has, in whose bytes the file is then named); with no locale, LC_ALL=C or a locale the system lacks, and on Alpine (musl), the connection failed instead. The configuration is not the default: TlsMode defaults to prefer, which checks no certificate.

OpenEMR before 8.5.0 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability in interface/billing/sl_eob_invoice.php, which escapes billing codes for HTML attributes but not for JavaScript strings in an inline onkeyup handler. Clinicians with encounter coding access can save crafted billing codes through diagnosis.php that execute script when a Back Office user enters a payment, exposing patient and financial data or performing actions as that user.

Local privilege escalation vulnerability in Iperius Backup 8.8.3, due to insufficient separation between the graphical user interface running with elevated privileges and local users with low privileges. When the backup service is configured to run persistently with Administrator privileges, a local attacker with low privileges can use the native Windows dialogues exposed by the application to run programmes that inherit its elevated context. This allows commands to be executed with SYSTEM or Administrator privileges, depending on the application’s context, and compromises the affected Windows system.
Memory overflow in KBA (knowledge-based authentication) can lead to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or Denial of Service in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway.

In Progress® Telerik® UI for ASP.NET Core versions `2015.1.318` through `2026.3.811`, repeated server-side aggregation requests, with or without grouping, cause dynamic assemblies and load contexts to be retained, resulting in accumulating process memory consumption. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this if the application exposes an aggregation endpoint that is reachable without authentication. Repeated requests can cause memory growth that may exhaust available resources and affect application availability. Disabling grouping in the client-side interface does not prevent direct requests containing these descriptors. The issue is fixed in version `2026.3.1015`.

In affected versions of Progress® Telerik® UI for ASP.NET MVC `2012.2.710` through `2026.3.811`, ClassFactory updates a shared class dictionary without exclusive write protection and emits non-collectible dynamic assemblies that remain loaded for the AppDomain's lifetime. The dictionary lookup and insertion are not atomic, and case variations in aggregate descriptors can produce distinct retained types even though member resolution is case-insensitive. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this if the application exposes an aggregation endpoint that is reachable without authentication, by submitting concurrent or repeated crafted requests. These requests may corrupt dictionary state or increase CPU and memory use, potentially degrading availability. The issue is fixed in version `2026.3.1015`.

A buffer over-read vulnerability in Fortinet FortiOS 7.4.0 through 7.4.3, FortiOS 7.2 all versions, FortiOS 7.0 all versions may allow an authenticated remote attacker to return a portion of device memory in the redirect response via submitting a specially crafted request.

The All in One SEO – AI SEO Plugin to Boost SEO Rankings & Traffic (Schema, Local SEO, Sitemap & SEO Insights) plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'name' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 5.0.5 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Successful exploitation requires that an administrator has placed the AIOSEO breadcrumb on the author template, that the site is running WordPress 6.6 or later with the core Interactivity runtime loaded (e.g., via a block theme or core/navigation block), and that a victim clicks the rendered breadcrumb link on the author archive page.

The Zephyr WebSocket client validates the server's handshake response in on_header_value() in subsys/net/lib/websocket/websocket.c. The comparison was performed as strncmp(at, str, length), where length is the length of the value the server sent rather than the length of the expected value, so the check only asked whether the received value was a prefix of the expected base64(SHA-1(key || GUID)). A server that returned a handful of correct characters passed, and a response carrying an empty Sec-WebSocket-Accept: header caused strncmp() to be called with a count of zero, which returns 0 and set ctx->sec_accept_ok with no comparison performed at all. The header-value callback also cleared ctx->sec_accept_present after the first chunk, so a value split across receive-buffer boundaries was only ever examined in part.

ctx->sec_accept_ok is the sole WebSocket-specific gate in websocket_connect(); the client does not check the HTTP status code or the Upgrade:/Connection: headers. Any HTTP response containing an empty or prefix-matching Sec-WebSocket-Accept header therefore completed the handshake, after which the socket is finalized as a WebSocket and all further peer bytes are parsed as frames. The affected path is driven directly by remote input through subsys/net/lib/http/http_parser.c, and is reached by every user of websocket_connect(), including MQTT over WebSocket (subsys/net/lib/mqtt/mqtt_transport_websocket.c) and subsys/net/lib/ocpp/ocpp.c.

The Sec-WebSocket-Accept exchange is not a secret-based authentication -- an endpoint or on-path attacker that sees the request can compute the expected value -- so the impact is bounded to parties that never observed the handshake request: a caching or transparent intermediary replaying a canned response, an off-path attacker injecting a spoofed response, or a non-WebSocket endpoint the client was induced to talk to. For those, the per-connection binding that RFC 6455 requires the client to enforce provided no protection at all, letting a single crafted response convince the device it holds a live WebSocket session and causing it to send application data to, and accept frames from, an unverified peer. There is no memory-safety consequence.

The fix compares each delivered chunk against the expected value at the position reached so far, refuses a chunk that would overrun it, and accepts only once every byte of the expected value -- and no more -- has been matched; on_header_field() now also clears the flag for any other header so a partial value cannot be continued across an intervening header.

The Synopsys DesignWare I3C controller driver (drivers/i3c/i3c_dw.c) tracks free Device Address Table (DAT) slots with get_free_pos(), which signals an exhausted table by returning -1. The helper declared its return type as uint8_t, so the sentinel was truncated to 255, and both consumers (dw_i3c_attach_device() and dw_i3c_i2c_attach_device()) also stored it in a uint8_t before testing if (pos < 0) — a comparison that is never true for an unsigned value. The exhaustion guard was therefore inert in every build.

With the guard defeated, an attach attempted on a full DAT proceeds with pos == 255: it writes data->dw_i3c_i2c_priv_data[255].id, more than 200 bytes past the end of the 32-element dw_i3c_i2c_priv_data array and past the end of struct dw_i3c_data; it stores the resulting out-of-bounds address in desc->controller_priv, from which later detach, reattach and IBI operations read the slot index back; and it performs a 32-bit MMIO store 1020 bytes beyond the hardware DAT base, outside the table the controller reports. The attach still returns success, so the upper layer believes the device is bound.

The DAT is smaller than the software array (its depth is read from DEVICE_ADDR_TABLE_POINTER, commonly 8 or 16 entries), so exhaustion is reachable. In a dual-role build (CONFIG_I3C_DUAL_ROLE with CONFIG_I3C_USE_IBI) acting as a secondary controller, the attach count is supplied by the bus's active controller: i3c_sec_handoffed() attaches one device per entry of the received DEFTGTS list, so a hostile or malfunctioning controller on the local I3C bus that declares more targets than the local DAT depth triggers the condition once per surplus entry. Exhaustion can also be reached from a devicetree that declares more devices than the table holds, or by repeated i3c attach shell commands.

Impact is bounded: the out-of-bounds store is a single byte of fixed value at a fixed displacement, with no attacker-chosen data or offset, so the realistic outcomes are corruption of neighbouring static driver state, writes into reserved controller registers, and inconsistent driver bookkeeping (a crash or a wedged I3C bus) rather than a controllable memory-write primitive. The attack vector is the local chip-to-chip I3C bus; there is no network-reachable path.

The Bluetooth Classic SDP server in subsys/bluetooth/host/classic/sdp.c allocated every response PDU through bt_sdp_create_pdu(), which expands to bt_l2cap_create_pdu() and therefore uses a K_FOREVER timeout. The allocation is made from sdp_pool, a fixed pool holding only CONFIG_BT_MAX_CONN buffers (one in the default configuration) that is shared with the SDP client role. When the pool is empty the call blocks without a bound.

The allocation is reached from bt_sdp_recv() on the Bluetooth host's RX context: the bt_workq "BT RX WQ" workqueue in the default configuration since v3.1.0, and the dedicated "BT RX" thread before that. This context processes all normal-priority HCI events and all received ACL data. The SDP L2CAP server is registered on PSM 0x0001 with no security requirement (BT_SECURITY_L0), so an unpaired, unauthenticated BR/EDR peer within radio range of a connectable device can drive it. Every malformed or unrecognised SDP PDU reaches send_err_rsp(), and the sdp_svc_search_req(), sdp_svc_att_req() and sdp_svc_search_att_req() handlers allocate as well, so a short burst of pipelined requests drains the pool and parks the RX context in the blocking allocation.

A pool buffer is released only once its response has been sent, and a peer that withholds baseband acknowledgements keeps the controller's buffers for the link full, so the response is never sent. While the RX context is blocked, the entire Bluetooth host, for all connections and both LE and BR/EDR, stops processing normal-priority HCI events and received data. In most affected releases the stall is permanent. Queued PDUs are freed only by connection or channel teardown, which waits for the normal-priority Disconnection Complete handler, and that handler runs on the blocked RX context, so the host does not recover without a reset. In v3.7.0 through v4.1.x the TX processor discards the queued response once the link supervision timeout drops the connection, so each stall ends at that timeout, but the peer can reconnect and repeat it for as long as it stays in range. The impact is limited to availability; no memory corruption or information disclosure is involved.

The fix adds sdp_svc_create_pdu() using K_NO_WAIT, pre-allocates the response buffer once in bt_sdp_recv(), stashes the request in sdp->recv_pending when no buffer is available, and retries it from a work handler once a buffer is freed by the pool destroy callback.

Faust.js is a headless WordPress toolkit. Prior to 1.8.12, the FaustWP generateAuthorizationCode GraphQL mutation called wp_authenticate_username_password and wp_authenticate_email_password directly instead of using wp_authenticate. This bypassed callbacks registered on WordPress's outer authenticate filter, including policies for multifactor authentication, single sign-on, IP allowlists, or disabled accounts. On a site using FaustWP local login and one of those policies, an attacker with a valid username or email and password could obtain an authorization code and exchange it through /api/faust/auth/token for access and refresh tokens even when the normal WordPress login path would deny access. This issue is fixed in version 1.8.12.

When Gitea acts as an OAuth2 or OpenID Connect provider, the token endpoint did not check the state of the user. After an administrator deactivated an account or prohibited its sign-in, existing refresh tokens and unused authorization codes of that user could still be exchanged for new tokens, so applications that sign users in through Gitea kept them signed in. The token endpoint now refuses users who may not sign in, and token introspection reports their tokens as inactive.

A Permission Model bypass in Node.js recursive file watching discloses the names of files and directories the process is not permitted to read. On macOS and Windows, fs.watch() and fs.promises.watch() in recursive mode are backed by the native libuv watcher: FSEventWrap::Start checks kFileSystemRead only once, on the watched root, and FSEventWrap::OnEvent then forwards every filename libuv reports (relative paths at any depth) to the JavaScript callback without checking that each path is covered by the read grant. Code running under --permission with an exact read grant on a directory can therefore learn names such as sub/secret.txt even though readdir on that subdirectory is denied. The flaw exposes names and timing metadata, not file contents, and requires macOS or Windows plus files created under the watched directory by another actor. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.
Incorrect permission assignment for critical resource in Azure Front Door (AFD) allows an unauthorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network.

The Libreswan IKEv2 state machine did not verify that an IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange was required to satisfy the addke= PostQuantum algorithm component of the exchange. A connecting client could (maliciously or by implementation error) skip the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange and start an IKE_AUTH exchange prematurely. The result is as if the addke= option had not been specified, and such connections are only protected by the classic key exchange algorithm (such as P-256 or Curve25519), allowing "store now, decrypt later" attacks once a quantum computer becomes available. Only connections with the addke= keyword in the ike= and/or esp= configuration option are affected. PostQuantum Hybrid Key Exchange support was added in version 5.4.
